 Senate Education and Labor Spending Bill Protects Pell Grants, Adult Basic Education, and Other Community College Priorities
 November 18, 2026
 Jonathan Elkin 
 Share this: 
 Twitter 
 Facebook 
 Linkedin 
 Email 
 On Monday night, the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee majority  released  a party-line Labor-Health and Human Services-Education(Labor-HHS-ED)bill for fiscal year 2027 (FY27), with the final five of 12 annual spending bills. 
 Good News
 Thanks to the advocacy of community college leaders at ACCT’s National Legislative Summit and all year, the Labor-HHS-ED bill would protect Pell Grants and other top priorities from cuts, while providing increases to some programs: 
 Pell Grants: Flat funding the maximumPell Grant award at $7,395, without cuts. This spring, community colleges helped earn a record-breaking number of Republicans and Democrats  publicly  supporting Pell Grant funding . The bill provides $15 billion to shore up the Pell Grant shortfall created by Congress’s bipartisan FAFSA Simplification Act of 2020, which increased FAFSA completion, eligibility, and student beneficiaries. 
 Adult Basic Education (ABE): increase to $729,167,000 ($13,712,000 or 1.9% increase). In contrast, President Trump’s budget and the House Republican bill proposedcompletely eliminatingABE. 38 bipartisan senators  publicly supported  ABE funding this year. 
 Strengthening Community Colleges Training Grants (SCCTG):  $70,000,000 ($5million or7.7% increase). This spring, a record 10 bipartisan senators  publicly supported  SCCTG funding.  
 Child Care Access Means Parents in School (CCAMPIS): $75,000,000 (Level funding). The bill includes language directing future grantees to provide data on parenting students and the number served in CCAMPIS, and helping students find otherchild careand support services.  
 Perkins Career and Technical Education (CTE):  $1,462,269,000 ($22,421,000 or 1.6% increase).  
 Apprenticeships:  $20 million or 7% increase. 
 Federal TRIO Programs:  $1,197,000,000 ($6 million or 0.5% increase). The bill language would require that ED “shall administer such programs consistent with prior practice and congressional intent to prevent disruption,” and sets deadlines to release the next grant competition and make new and continuing awards. The explanatory statement encourages Educational Opportunity Centers for justice-involved individuals. 
 Gaining Early Awareness and Readiness for Undergraduate Programs (GEAR UP):  $393 million ($5 million or 1.3% increase). The explanatory statement would require ED to provide at least 33% to State grants (with no more than one State grant at a time) and at least 33% to Partnership Grants in which colleges can apply directly.  
 Strengthening Institutions Program (SIP), Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs), Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), and Tribally Controlled Colleges and Universities (TCCUs):  The bill provides level funding to these programs without cuts. Note that the bill stays silent on the Trump Administration’s actions to move funding from MSIs to these other programs 
 Federal Work-Study and Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grants (SEOG):  $1,230,000 and $910,000,000, respectively (Level funding) 
 Earmarks for Community Colleges: Community colleges advocated successfully to include many earmarks in these proposed bills. For each bill, you can search the Explanatory Statements, which have a table with a list of proposed earmarks. ACCT staff will compile a list of all community college earmarks after final enactment of FY27 appropriations bills. To view community college earmarks from FY22-FY26, scroll to the bottom of ACCT's appropriations page  here . For tips on preparing earmark requests for next year, check  ACCT  Connect , our member-only resource page. 
 Beyond Labor-HHS-ED, last week’sbills protect two additional national programs for community colleges, without cuts: 
 Advanced Technological Education (ATE) within the National Science Foundation (NSF):  The  Commerce, Justice, and Science (CJS) Senate bill  proposes $75 million in level funding for NSF ATE. ACCT  advocated  to protect funding for the program this spring. 
 Tribally Controlled Colleges and Universities (TCCUs):  The  Department of the Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies bill  proposes $87,926,000 in level funding. ACCT joined the American Indian Higher Education Consortium (AIHEC) in  advocating  for TCCU funding within the Department of the Interior, and also for separate TCCU accounts in the Department of Education. 
  Needs Improvement
 Education Department General Administrative Regulations (EDGAR) Proposal:  The bill does not yet block the harmful Trump Administration proposal that would allow ED political staff to end competitive ED grants “for convenience.” This could be highly disruptive to many community colleges. Take Action!  See details and a sample message to Congress here . 
 Child Care Access Means Parents in School (CCAMPIS):  This spring, ED stated it planned to award 148 CCAMPIS grants for fiscal year 2026. 79 applicants earned a perfect score of 100, but ED only awarded 40 grants, even though there was enough money to make more awards. Over 100 community colleges ended their CCAMPIS grants as scheduled on September 30, 2026, and did not win a new grant to continue their awards. Take Action!  Urge Congress to immediately fund more FY26 applications in score order to fund more awards . 
 Pell Grant maximum and long-term outlook:  While the bill would protect Pell Grant funding for one year, the bill does not put Pell Grant funding on long-term stable financial footing or increase the maximum grant. Although themaximumPell Grant is enough to pay community college tuition and fees in most states, the grant has not kept up with inflation and falls far below the full cost of attendance, including food, housing, child care, and transportation.  
 International Education and Foreign Language Studies: $75,664,000 ($5,336,000 or 6.6% cut). Note that President Trump’s budget and the House bill would completely zero out funding. 
 What Happens Next?  
 Federal spending is now under a continuing resolution (CR), or temporary flat funding, until December 11. Top Democrats and Republicans in the House and Senate are negotiating on final topline funding levels for defense and domestic spending–including the Iran war–before they make allocations for each of the 12 bills or individual programs. This week’sSenate Republican-only bills let staff begin to negotiate various scenarios behind the scenes, so they are ready to process bill text quickly after leaders reach decisions on toplines. The final bills must be passed by the full House and Senate, then signed by the President, to be enacted into law. Congress could pass another short-term CR into the new calendar year, when Democrats will have control of both the House and Senate. If Congress does not pass at least a short-term extension, there could be a shutdown.
